candidate.answerReason: The region has area 11. The bisecting line must have slope between 1/3 and 1; in this range its lower portion has area \(2+9m/2\). Equating this to \(11/2\) gives the admissible slope \(m=7/9\), choice E.

methods.label: Split the lower area into a rectangle and a triangle
methods.explanation:
Split the L-shaped region into the square \(0\leq x\leq3\), \(0\leq y\leq3\), and the rectangle \(3\leq x\leq5\), \(0\leq y\leq1\). Their interiors do not overlap, and together they fill the region. Its total area is
\[
3\cdot3+2\cdot1=11,
\]
so each half must have area \(11/2\).

A vertical line through the origin, or a line of nonpositive slope, leaves the entire interior of this first-quadrant region on one side. Thus the required line has positive slope \(m\) and equation \(y=mx\).

First determine where the line exits the square. If \(m\leq1/3\), the area below it within the square is at most the triangle of base \(3\) and height \(1\). Even including the entire right rectangle, the lower area is at most
\[
\frac12\cdot3\cdot1+2=\frac72<\frac{11}{2}.
\]
If \(m\geq1\), the lower area contains at least half the square and all of the right rectangle, giving at least
\[
\frac92+2=\frac{13}{2}>\frac{11}{2}.
\]
Consequently, \(1/3<m<1\).

In this range the line meets \(x=3\) at \((3,3m)\), with \(1<3m<3\). The part below it consists exactly of a triangle inside the square, with base \(3\) and height \(3m\), together with the entire right rectangle. These pieces have disjoint interiors, so the required equation is
\[
\frac12\cdot3\cdot3m+2=\frac{11}{2}.
\]
Thus \(9m+4=11\), giving \(m=7/9\). This lies strictly between \(1/3\) and \(1\), so the area description applies and confirms that the line bisects the region. The excluded ranges cannot work, and the equation in the remaining range has only this solution. The slope is \(\boxed{\frac79}\), choice \(\mathrm{E}\).

review.mathematicalCheck: The coordinate region has area 9+2=11. Vertical and nonpositive-slope lines cannot bisect it. For positive slopes m≤1/3 the lower area is at most 7/2; for m≥1 it is at least 13/2. In the remaining range the lower area is exactly 2+9m/2. Equating it to 11/2 yields m=7/9, within that range, proving existence and uniqueness. The decomposition agrees with the displayed figure.
